flashcards.q: What is the NodePort default port range, and what does externalTrafficPolicy: Local trade away?
flashcards.a: 30000-32767. Local avoids the extra cross-node hop by only forwarding to same-node pods, but a node with no local pod for that Service simply drops traffic that lands there — trading even load distribution for hop-avoidance and real source IP preservation.

flashcards.q: kube-proxy modes: what's the current default, what replaced it for scale, and what's now deprecated?
flashcards.a: iptables is still the default (O(n) chain walk, slow at scale). IPVS (O(1) hash table) was added to fix that but is deprecated as of Kubernetes 1.35. nftables (stable since 1.33, atomic rule replacement) is the intended long-term replacement but is NOT yet the default, for compatibility reasons.

flashcards.q: What's the default NetworkPolicy posture with zero policy objects, and what changes the moment one policy selects a pod?
flashcards.a: Default is allow-all in both directions. The moment any NetworkPolicy selects a pod for a given direction (ingress or egress), that direction flips to default-deny for that pod except what's explicitly allowed — but only that direction, not both.
Writing an ingress-only policy and assuming egress is now also restricted — it isn't. Egress stays fully open until a separate policy explicitly selects that pod for the egress direction too.

flashcards.q: Does the Kubernetes API server enforce NetworkPolicy objects?
flashcards.a: No. NetworkPolicy objects are just stored, schema-validated data unless the cluster's CNI implements a policy controller. Plain Flannel enforces nothing by default — policies can look correctly applied via kubectl while having zero actual effect on traffic.

flashcards.q: What is ndots:5 and why does it slow down external API calls from pods?
flashcards.a: Default resolv.conf setting: any hostname with fewer than 5 dots gets every in-cluster search suffix tried in order before an absolute lookup. A call like api.stripe.com (2 dots) triggers up to 4 failed internal lookups before the correct 5th (bare) lookup succeeds — up to ~5x latency on cold external DNS lookups.

flashcards.q: Two fixes for the ndots DNS latency problem?
flashcards.a: Trailing-dot known-external hostnames in code (fully-qualifies them, skips the search list), or tune ndots down via pod.spec.dnsConfig for latency-sensitive workloads; NodeLocal DNSCache also helps by absorbing repeat lookups per node.

flashcards.q: Why is ingress-nginx's retirement significant, and is the Ingress API itself dying?
flashcards.a: No — SIG-Network says the core Ingress API will be maintained indefinitely. What's retiring is the specific ingress-nginx controller implementation: best-effort maintenance only through March 2026, then read-only archival with no further fixes.

flashcards.q: What's the core structural fix Gateway API provides over Ingress?
flashcards.a: Role-oriented separation: GatewayClass/Gateway are infra-team-owned, HTTPRoute is app-team-owned, with native traffic splitting and header-based routing as first-class fields — versus Ingress's thin spec (host/path/TLS only) that pushes everything else into non-portable, controller-specific annotations.

flashcards.q: Why did EndpointSlices replace the single Endpoints object?
flashcards.a: A Service with thousands of pods meant any single pod IP change required rewriting/re-propagating one giant Endpoints object. EndpointSlices shard endpoints (~100 per slice by default) so a single change only updates and propagates the one small slice containing it.

flashcards.q: How does a headless Service's DNS answer differ from a normal ClusterIP Service's?
flashcards.a: ClusterIP returns one A record for the virtual IP (backing pod opaque to client). Headless (clusterIP: None) returns individual pod IPs directly plus SRV records for IP+port discovery per pod — no load balancing at all, client chooses which address to use.

flashcards.q: Why does Cilium's eBPF dataplane scale differently than iptables, not just 'faster'?
flashcards.a: iptables cost grows roughly linearly (O(n)) with rule count via sequential chain walks. eBPF compiles policies into in-kernel maps with near-constant/logarithmic lookup cost — a different growth curve, so the gap becomes dramatic specifically at high Service/policy counts (often cited around 1,000+) rather than being a fixed multiplier at every scale.
